newsitem.title: UK: Questions remain on U.S.-British special ties.
newsitem.headline: Questions remain on U.S.-British special ties.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton left Britain after triumphantly parading his friendship with new Prime Minister Tony Blair but questions remain about how much of the "special relationship" between the two countries really remains.

The flurry of handshakes and sea of smiles on Thursday showed how much more comfortable Clinton looked in the company of Blair than predecessor John Major, whose seven-year tenure marked a low in transatlantic relations.
Blair and Clinton showed some of their new-found confidence by announcing a joint initiative to tackle unemployment under the umbrella of the Group of Seven industrialised countries.

But experts say the days when Britain could really consider itself to be Washington's key partner, acting both as a bridge between Europe and the United States and as a faithful partner in defence during the Cold War, have gone.

"A country like the United States has special relationships with everyone in the world. The concept is nonsense," said Dr Jonathan Eyal, director of studies at the Royal United Services Institute think-tank.

Britain energetically pushed the idea in the 1980s when former prime minister Margaret Thatcher and President Ronald Reagan forged what looked to be an unbreakable friendship but which did not always live up to expectations.
"There was always a large element of hype to the special relationship," Eyal said in a telephone interview.
"When it didn't suit the United States to tell Britain something, it kept quiet. A good example was the 1983 invasion of Grenada -- a member of the British Commonwealth."

The United States once looked instinctively to London when dealing with Europe but gradually broadened its gaze, especially when deep divisions within Major's Conservatives over policy towards the European Union increasingly marginalised Britain.

"Washington sees Europe as much more of a large blob these days and is looking for a foreign policy that's good for the entire continent rather than concentrating on a few individual nations," said a political analyst at one western embassy.

Blair has already taken several steps to end the battles with the EU, saying Washington would only prize deep relations with a Britain at the heart of Europe. Some question whether at heart the Labour administration is paying much attention.

"This is probably the most Europeanised cabinet there's ever been and they need much less the transatlantic prop with which to reassure themselves," said Christopher Hitchens, an observer at Vanity Fair magazine.
"There is no issue between Britain and America at the moment that requires the chemistry to be good," he told independent Channel Four television.
Eyal said that despite the end of the Cold War, London and Washington retained close defence links.

"There are areas where the relationship continues unimpeded. Britain is the only country which receives all the raw intelligence data from the United States. They work very closely together," he said.
"The level of cooperation in defence procurement and production is unprecedented. It is hugely important."

Colonel Terry Taylor, deputy director of the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said Britain still had plenty of influence, especially over the future of the international peacekeeping force in Bosnia.

"Europe will want the Americans to stay beyond the deadline of June 1998 and the best people to persuade them are the British, who do not take the aggressive stance of the French," he said in an interview.
